report:
## Conclusion

The claim that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19 is **false**. There is no scientific evidence supporting this claim, and it has been repeatedly debunked by public health authorities and fact-checkers.

The World Health Organization explicitly addressed this in its COVID-19 "Mythbusters" series, stating that while garlic is a healthy food with some antimicrobial properties, "there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters).

AFP Fact Check similarly investigated viral claims about garlic (often combined with onion, ginger, and lemon) as a COVID-19 cure and found "no evidence for its use as an effective treatment," with health professionals confirming this as early as February 2020 (https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19).

Rappler's fact-checking team also rated a related claim—that heat, garlic, and ginger can prevent or cure COVID-19—as **False**, noting there is no official cure or preventive treatment for the disease outside of vaccines and approved medical treatments (https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/264621-heat-garlic-ginger-cure-covid-19/).

No peer-reviewed clinical trials have demonstrated that garlic, in any preparation, eliminates or cures SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans. While garlic contains compounds with mild antimicrobial properties in laboratory settings, this does not translate to curing an active viral infection like COVID-19 in the human body.

**Bottom line:** Drinking boiled garlic water may be a harmless dietary habit, but it does not cure, treat, or prevent COVID-19. Anyone suspecting infection should rely on vaccination, antiviral medications prescribed by physicians, and guidance from legitimate health authorities rather than home remedies.
